equivalents.note: The Tibetan line reads differently, brtse ba med pas baM ga la yul khyer, 'pitilessly carried off the land of Baṃgala': it takes adaa- as 'without compassion' (a-daya), not Munidatta's advaya, and makes Baṅgāla what is carried off rather than where, or by whom, the afflictions are plundered.

The Tibetan does not say 'Bengali' but nang 'khrug shor, 'inner strife broke out', and it puts nang 'khrug for vaṅgālikā in the comment too (cp.49.m1, cp.49.m3), so this is its consistent reading of the word, not a literal rendering.
The Tibetan gives only 'the five kinds', leaving -dhāṭa untranslated, and keeps the same phrase where Munidatta cites pañcapāṭana (cp.49.m4).

The Tibetan takes caukoṛi as a number, four ten-millions, not as Munidatta's four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi), which its comment renders mtha' bzhi while still citing the line as bye ba phrag bzhi (cp.49.m6).
The quoted verse's saṅkalpa ('imagining the afflictions') is rendered by the bare verb rtog, not the comment's usual rnam par rtog pa.
The Tibetan verse line 2b has the same gtum pos khyer, 'carried off by the fierce one', where Shastri's Bengali reads caṇḍālī, so the Tibetan agrees with Munidatta's masculine caṇḍālena.
Here 'the words (tshig) of the dhru', not the comment's usual d+h+rU'i rkang pa.
The same verb renders the verse's ḍahi in 3a (bsregs shing), which the comment cites here.
The Tibetan verse 3b already has rang sems rin chen, 'my own mind-jewel', where the Bengali has only cia mora, 'my mind', in line with Munidatta's cittaratna here.
Beside gser in the cited lemma, the comment transcribes Munidatta's sona as so na, and its rU pa for his [ta]ruya suggests a source reading rūpā, 'silver', which would explain dngul in 4a.
The Tibetan has blo rmongs pa, 'dull-minded', for mūḍhadhīḥ.
In the verse (1b) the Tibetan instead renders adaa-, which Munidatta takes as advaya, as brtse ba med pas, 'pitilessly', as if from a-daya.
Here the comment renders the Vaṅgāla of advayavaṅgāla as nang 'khrug pa, 'the one of inner strife', its word for baṅgālī in 2a, not the transcribed baM ga la of 1b and cp.49.m2.

questions: canal (cp.49.1a): not matched. The Tibetan line has rgyal po'i gru ni pad+ma'i tshal nas 'bab, 'the king's boat comes down from the lotus grove'; tshal, 'grove', stands where the Bengali has khālem̐, 'on the canal', but does not render it, so I give no equivalent.
klesa (cp.49.1b): not matched. The Tibetan line (brtse ba med pas baM ga la yul khyer) has no word for the afflictions; the term is already matched in cp.49.m2 (nyon mongs).

candali (cp.49.2b): not matched. gtum pos is masculine and agentive, 'by the fierce one', so the Tibetan reads Caṇḍāla, as Munidatta's caṇḍālena does, not Shastri's caṇḍālī; I give gtum pos under candala (cp.49.m3) instead. Should candala also be linked at 2b?

mahasukha (cp.49.4b): not matched. The Tibetan line has rang gi 'khor gyis rin chen blangs nas gnas, 'my own retinue took the jewel and stays', with no word for great bliss; rin chen, 'jewel', echoes Munidatta's mahāsukharatna. The term is already matched in the comment (cp.49.m4, cp.49.m5).

atyantabhava (cp.49.m6): not matched. Where the Sanskrit has caturthapadenātyantābhāvam āha, the Tibetan has rkang pa bzhi pas shin tu bsgoms pa gsungs te, 'the fourth verse speaks of thorough meditation', apparently reading atyanta-bhāvanā; shin tu bsgoms pa does not render 'absolute nonexistence' (the glossary's shin tu med pa), so I give no equivalent.
